Bad Limit

LimitsParadoxesSequences
Game: This is a picture to explore, not a game to win: a big square, a smaller square inside it, and a zigzag line that follows the smaller one.
How to play: Move the slider or press the arrow buttons to change how many little steps the zigzag has. Watch what happens to its length.
5
Look for the math

A picture can creep closer and closer to a shape without its length creeping closer too. This applet is the classic example: the zigzag looks more and more like the small square, yet its length never changes.

Two squares

Let the big square have side L, so its perimeter is S = 4L. Joining the midpoints of its sides makes the small diamond. The distance between two neighbouring midpoints is L/√2, so the small square's perimeter is

s = 4L/√2 = S/√2 ≈ 0.71 S

The cut-the-knot page says s = S/2. That is not right for a midpoint square: the true factor is 1/√2, about 0.71 rather than 0.5. The logic test checks this directly.

A staircase on a diamond side

Put r = L/2, half the big square's side. One side of the diamond is the diagonal of an r-by-r square, so it is r√2 long. The zigzag instead goes across by r and down by r in little steps. Its horizontal pieces add to r and its vertical pieces add to r, giving 2r per side. Four sides make

sn = 4 × 2r = 8r = S

That does not depend on how many steps you use: the small steps still add up to the same r across and r down. This is the invariant behind the whole picture.

More steps, same length

The logic test checks every value the applet allows, n = 1 to 105: in each case sn = S. So the limit of the lengths is S, not s. The curves really do converge — the furthest the zigzag strays from the diamond shrinks like r/(n√2) — but their lengths stay at S. Converging pictures need not have converging lengths.

Why the circle is different

Archimedes estimated a circle's circumference with inscribed polygons, and there the polygon lengths do approach the circumference. A circle is smooth: its edges settle down to the curve. Here the zigzag keeps making sharp right-angle detours at every size, so the extra length never disappears. That gap is the paradox.

Try 1 break point, then 105. The picture looks very different, but the zigzag's length never moves.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
